item.title: Grizzly HTTP Server
item.description:
Grizzly is a Java NIO networking framework maintained by the Eclipse EE4J project. Its grizzly-framework module builds on Java’s non-blocking I/O APIs; it is not a direct wrapper around a particular operating-system API such as epoll.

Modules #

Common Grizzly modules include:

  • grizzly-http, which provides HTTP protocol support;
  • grizzly-http-server, an embeddable HTTP server with Grizzly’s own API; and
  • grizzly-http-servlet, which provides servlet-related integration.

Grizzly is used by GlassFish and can also run small embedded services. It is an HTTP server, not a Jakarta REST implementation. Combine it with Jersey when serving JAX-RS resources.

item.title: HTTP Video Streaming
item.description: HTTP video delivery ranges from one seekable file to an adaptive sequence of short media segments. HTTP moves representations and validators; a container organizes timed tracks, and codecs encode the audio and video samples. Keeping those layers separate makes range handling, caching, and playback failures easier to diagnose.

item.title: Curl
item.description: curl transfers a URL with an ordered command line: options configure one or more transfers, and every URL starts a transfer. It supports many protocols; examples below use HTTP because its request and response controls are common.

item.title: Browser Content Disposition and Downloads
item.description:
Browsers decide whether to display a response, download it, or hand it to an external application from several inputs. Content-Disposition provides a strong preference, but content type, navigation context, sandboxing, browser capabilities, and user settings also affect the result.

Inline and Attachment Dispositions #

An attachment response requests a download:

http 
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/pdf
Content-Disposition: attachment; filename="guide.pdf"
Content-Length: 110352
X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff

An inline response permits presentation inside the browser:

http 
Content-Type: application/pdf
Content-Disposition: inline; filename="guide.pdf"

inline does not guarantee display. The browser needs a viewer for the media type, and the user can configure some types to download instead. Omitting the header leaves the choice primarily to the media type and navigation context.

item.title: Server-Driven HTTP Traffic
item.description:
Server-driven HTTP lets a server send information without a new client request for every update. Server-Sent Events (SSE) is a simple standardized option for one-way server-to-browser updates.

Server-Sent Events #

An SSE client makes a normal GET request with an Accept: text/event-stream header. The server replies with 200 OK, Content-Type: text/event-stream, and keeps the response open while sending UTF-8 event fields separated by a blank line:

text 
event: order-updated
id: 42
data: {"status":"paid"}

In browsers, EventSource reconnects automatically. The server can send retry: to suggest a reconnection delay, and the browser sends Last-Event-ID after a reconnect when an event ID was received. Design the stream so clients can resume from that ID or refresh a snapshot safely.

item.title: CDN Origin Routing
item.description:
CDN routing has two separate decisions: where a client connects and which origin the edge contacts. DNS and anycast choose an edge location; configuration at that edge chooses an origin and constructs the upstream request. Keeping those decisions separate makes failures easier to diagnose.

Request Identity at the Edge #

A client starts with a URL such as https://www.example.com/docs. DNS returns an edge address, TLS SNI identifies www.example.com during the handshake, and the HTTP request carries Host: www.example.com (or the equivalent :authority field in HTTP/2 and HTTP/3). The CDN uses this hostname and path to select a distribution and cache behavior.
